source.title: Disentangling Dense Embeddings with Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Charles O'Neill; Christine Ye; Kartheik G. Iyer; John F. Wu

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper and appendices through the end of Appendix G; no apparent truncation affects the reported findings below.
record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse autoencoders to dense scientific-text embeddings and reports feature interpretability and cross-capacity/domain feature comparisons, extending the subject to a new representation setting rather than reproducing the toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that an SAE recovers interpretable sparse features from embeddings, and measures how feature matches vary across SAE capacities and domains. It does not test toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions or test competition for neuron capacity. SAE search-intervention results are not included because they assess the search method, not the claim versions. General reconstruction scaling metrics are also outside the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Trains top-k SAEs on dense LLM-derived text embeddings (OpenAI text-embedding-3-small) for astro-ph and cs.LG abstracts. It reports three kinds of result: how interpretable the recovered sparse features are (V4); whether features recur, split or misalign across SAE sizes and domains (V5); and, in an appendix, whether feature families are multi-dimensional manifolds (V6). This applies the claim to a new setting rather than reproducing the toy-model method.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs extract interpretable sparse features from dense scientific-text embeddings while keeping semantic fidelity, and that feature families give a multi-scale view. Features split and become more granular with capacity, with recurrent and novel features. Cross-domain SAEs share a small semi-universal subset amid broad misalignment. SAE features also allow precise steering of semantic search.
record.recipe_differences: Uses top-k sparse autoencoders trained on dense text embeddings and automated feature interpretation; does not reproduce the toy-model setup or its measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature similarity varies with SAE active-latent count k and total latent count n; feature alignment also varies across astro-ph and cs.LG training domains. The authors report Pearson interpretability correlations changing with k and n.

fits_no_version.finding: Encoder–decoder cosine similarity averages 0.57 (SAE64, cs.LG). It correlates negatively with a feature's maximum decoder similarity to other features, which the authors attribute to interference from superposition. The decoder matrix shows no block-diagonal clustering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In SAEs on dense embeddings, features that sit closer to other features need encoder directions that depart further from their decoder directions, consistent with interference from non-orthogonal superposed features.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says embeddings, trained SAEs, interpreted features, and a web app are open sourced, but the supplied text omits their URLs)
record.problems: Interpretability is assessed using LLM-generated feature descriptions and an LLM Predictor rather than ground-truth features. The authors note they do not use the full spectrum of activations, and that their domains are narrow. Cross-domain feature comparisons include only selected matches; numerical nearest-neighbour distributions are primarily presented in figures.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant results omitted. General SAE reconstruction-loss scaling, search-intervention accuracy, and search-query fidelity were left out because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy network, no sparsity-dependent transition, no geometry analysis of a model with known features.
All of it: no neuron-level capacity competition and no importance-dependent allocation of dimensions.
All of it: no alternative causes of polysemanticity are examined.
No measurement that features are spread across many embedding dimensions or neurons; this is asserted in the background only. Only one embedding model is studied, not internal LLM activations.
Completeness against ground-truth features is not tested; the authors list this as future work.
Only feature families from SAE64 are projected (three examples shown). Single features and other multi-dimensional structures are not examined in general.

missing.what: Cross-domain max cosine similarity distributions: the vast majority of features are misaligned between astro-ph and cs.LG SAEs, with misalignment increasing with k and n.
Self-consistency of nearest-neighbour matching SAE16→SAE64 direct vs via SAE32: set overlap is bimodal, mostly 0–0.6, and only small sets show perfect overlap.
Engels et al. projection of feature families: not manifolds or irreducible multi-dimensional structures.
Novel SAE64 features (e.g., LTB models, Lyman Break Galaxies) with no related feature in smaller SAEs, so smaller SAEs may not cover the feature space.

record.verdict_notes: Setting is an embedding model's output vectors, not internal LLM activations. Interpretability depends on an LLM judge, and the gpt-3.5 Predictor sharply lowers Pearson (Appendix C.3). Search-intervention results correctly excluded as method performance. Not an original source, so verdicts apply.

versions.untested_parts: No toy network superposition experiment, sparsity-dependent transition, or test of regular feature geometry.
No test of neuron-level capacity competition, dedicated dimensions for important features, or polysemantic neurons.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
Tests SAE-recoverable features in dense text embeddings from one embedding model and two scientific domains; does not measure feature spreading across neurons in an LLM’s internal activations.
Tests feature interpretability and similarity across SAE capacities and embedding domains, but does not establish completeness or canonical status against ground-truth model units.
Does not test whether the underlying model’s represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional or multidimensional.

source_check.reason: Sections 3.1–3.3 report recovered sparse features with median label-based prediction correlations of 0.85–0.98 for astro-ph and 0.65–0.71 for cs.LG (r1, r2). This supports recovery in the tested embedding setting; neuron participation is untested.

relationships.condition: Across SAE capacities (k, n) trained on the same data

relationships.display_finding: Nearest-neighbour similarity fell and novel non-split features appeared as k and n grew; recurrent triplets exceeded 1100 at k=16 but dropped sharply at higher k, and self-consistency overlap was bimodal, mostly 0–0.6.

source_check.notes: Appendix E.1 contains a contradictory higher-k phrase immediately before explicitly reporting declining triplet counts as k increases. Appendix D's stated mean cosine similarity of 0.59 does not equal the arithmetic mean of the eight displayed Table 4 cosine values; r37 faithfully records the stated aggregate.

statements.correction: Appendix E.2 and Figure 20: PCA projections of three SAE64 feature families; authors identify linear subspaces rather than manifolds or irreducible multidimensional structures. Abstract and introduction: open-source embeddings, trained SAEs, interpreted features and web application announced. Appendix C.3: Interpreter/Predictor model ablations on 50 astro-ph SAE64 features. No random-label or raw-dimension interpretability baseline stated.
statements.problem: The geometry and selected-family restriction are supported. Although the header is accurately described, its no-code/no-controls characterization needs qualification against the paper's announced open-source artifacts and judge ablations.
